roles.name: the application database role (NAME NOT STATED IN ANY DOCUMENT)
granted: ordinary DML on every other table (implied by the application working; never enumerated in any document)
connect via DATABASE_URL, which is the only connection string the application, the worker and the migrate command all read
denied: UPDATE on audit_log - 'UPDATE audit_log SET action = 'x' issued as that role raises a permission error'
DELETE on audit_log - 'DELETE FROM audit_log as that role raises the same permission error'
SUPERUSER - 'SELECT rolsuper FROM pg_roles WHERE rolname = current_user returns false when connected with the local compose stack's DATABASE_URL'
roles.cite: PRD E8 S7.3 'Audit: same transaction, append-only, before and after'; PRD E8 P-XCT-03; PRD E6 P-ADM-19 (E6_admin.md:2530); PRD E7 P-RPT-04 preconditions (E7_dashboard.md:919); PRD E8 S7.11 'Migrations'; PRD E8 P-XCT-20; FR-ADR-019; FR-ADR-062; SRC-002 §7.8; GOTCHAS.md 'Database & Postgres' first entry; Bible S-XCT-07; Bible S-XCT-33; Bible S-ADM-02
roles.why: Two separate reasons converge on one role. (1) Append-only audit: 'An audit log the application can rewrite is not evidence.' The grant is written IN THE MIGRATION and is checkable - Bible S-XCT-07 asserts SELECT privilege_type FROM information_schema.table_privileges WHERE table_name = 'audit_log' AND grantee = current_user returns EXACTLY the two rows INSERT and SELECT, and that UPDATE/DELETE raise SQLSTATE 42501 insufficient_privilege while SELECT and INSERT succeed as the same role. (2) RDS parity: 'Local PostgreSQL gives you superuser and RDS never does, so a migration that works locally can fail on RDS on superuser, forced SSL, or the allowed extension list. The compose stack creates an application role without superuser so the difference is caught on a laptop instead of during a deploy.' Bible S-XCT-33 turns that into a runnable assertion against the local compose stack.

conventions.rule: Primary keys are `bigint` identity columns - `GENERATED ALWAYS AS IDENTITY` - on EVERY table. Not uuid, not bigserial. `GENERATED ALWAYS AS IDENTITY` rather than `serial` is deliberate: 'the sequence is owned by the column and cannot be written to by accident. That is the stricter option and under Art III.10 needs no signature.' `integer` is explicitly rejected (nothing is ever deleted, so 2.1 billion is a ceiling that exists for no reason). UUIDv4, UUIDv7/ULID, a parallel public-uuid column, and natural keys are each named and rejected.
conventions.note: *** THIS CONTRADICTS THE BRIEF. *** The brief's type vocabulary says 'Primary keys are `uuid` with no database-side default unless a document says otherwise (the application generates ids; say so if your source disagrees).' A document says otherwise, on every table. Ids are GENERATED BY THE DATABASE, not by the application. FR-ADR-017's central argument is the correctness guard itself: 'The oversell guard is a unique index on (showtime_id, seat_id). Two 8-byte integers make a 16-byte key; two UUIDs make a 32-byte key on the single most contended index in the system.' The PRD and the Bible are consistent with this everywhere - every id in every worked example and every endpoint contract is an integer (showtime 41, seat 312, booking_id 9008, user_id 4471, 'showtime_id': 'integer', 'seat_id': 'integer'). Any cluster that returned `uuid` primary keys must be corrected at merge, and the merge owner should assume the five other clusters were given the same wrong default.

conventions.rule: No internal id appears in any URL, response body or interface element a customer can see, FOR PRIVATE OBJECTS. The private objects are bookings, payments, users and audit rows. A booking is addressed by its reference (FR-ADR-015), never by its primary key. Movies, showtimes, screens and seats ARE addressed by their internal id, because the seat map is already public to guests. Users are addressed by nothing public - a customer reads their own bookings through their session, never through a user id in a path.
conventions.note: Consequence recorded in the ADR: showtime and seat ids are enumerable, which makes the seat-map endpoint scrapeable - 'a rate-limiting concern rather than an authorisation one (FR-ADR-058).'

conventions.rule: 'Every timestamp column is `timestamptz`. Every stored value is UTC. Every rendered value is converted to Asia/Kolkata at the boundary. There is no `timestamp without time zone` anywhere in the schema.'
conventions.cite: FR-ADR-018; PRD E8 S7.19; ADR ledger LED-018
conventions.note: The zone is on the `cinema` row as an IANA name, NOT in application configuration: 'It costs one column.' FR-ADR-018 rejects putting it in config as the weaker option. India's fixed +05:30 is recorded as a fact about the zone, 'not a licence to hardcode +05:30'.

conventions.rule: 'Every table carries `created_at`; tables that mutate carry `updated_at`.' Restated in FR-ADR-012: 'Every table therefore needs `created_at`, and the tables that mutate need `updated_at`, because the history is the only thing that explains a row's current state.'
conventions.cite: PRD E8 P-XCT-04 preconditions (E8_crosscutting.md:307); FR-ADR-012 Consequences
conventions.note: created_at is universal and settled. updated_at is NOT settled per table, and the Bible says so in terms: 'Note for the implementer, not an acceptance criterion: tables that are edited after creation are expected to carry updated_at as well as created_at; which tables those are is a judgement that follows from the data model and is checked there rather than here' (Bible S-XCT-06, FrontRow_Bible.csv line 171). That judgement is explicitly handed to GOAL_08. See gaps.

conventions.topic: timestamps - database default vs injected clock
conventions.rule: '`created_at` and `updated_at` are `timestamptz` and default to `now()` at the database, which is always UTC. The injected clock governs domain decisions; the database clock governs row metadata. Those are deliberately different and the difference is why a test can control expiry without having to control the database.'
conventions.note: THE TENSION THE BRIEF ASKED ABOUT IS ALREADY NAMED AND ALREADY RESOLVED - it is not an undiscovered contradiction. FR-ADR-018 states both halves in the same paragraph: 'Time is injected. Domain code takes a clock; it never calls the system clock directly. A test that reads the wall clock is a defect (Art IX.5)' AND `DEFAULT now()` on row metadata. The split is: a database default is permitted ONLY on created_at/updated_at, which no assertion in the product depends on; every instant a decision is made against - hold expiry, the sales cut-off, 'today', password-reset expiry, dashboard period boundaries - is computed from the injected clock and STORED BY THE APPLICATION, never defaulted. Two consequences the merge owner must carry into the DDL: (a) do NOT put `DEFAULT now()` on any decision-bearing instant column (showtime.starts_at, showtime.ends_at, password_reset_token.expires_at, payment.pending_at/authorized_at/captured_at, audit_log.occurred_at, receipt_dispatch timestamps) - a defaulted decision instant is unreachable by an injected clock and a test asserting against it becomes a wall-clock test; (b) audit_log.occurred_at in particular is written by the application inside the same transaction as the change, and E8 S7.3 already forbids the trigger route for the same table ('Not a trigger. A database trigger cannot know the acting user or the request id - it sees a connection - and both are the point').

conventions.rule: '`bigint` in persistence. Every money column is an integer count of paise. `bigint` rather than `integer` because nothing is deleted and revenue totals accumulate; a 2.1-billion-paise ceiling is Rs 21,474,836, which is reachable and exists for no reason.' 'The naming convention is part of the rule. A field named `price` holding `250.00` is a defect; the field is `price_paise` and holds `25000`. A suffix on every money identifier is the cheapest way to make a unit error visible in a code review.' 'No float, anywhere, at any layer.' 'Decimal at the boundary only... There is no Decimal on the money path beyond that boundary.'
conventions.cite: PRD E8 S7.2 'Money: integer paise, one function, one one-way door'; FR-ADR-036; Bible S-PAY-01
conventions.note: Bible S-PAY-01 makes the type machine-checkable: 'SELECT column_name, data_type FROM information_schema.columns WHERE table_schema = 'public' AND table_name IN ('booking','booking_seat','payment') AND column_name LIKE '%_paise' returns exactly total_paise, price_paise, base_price_paise_applied, amount_paise and every data_type is bigint'. NUMERIC(x,2) is excluded by the type; the ADR's own rejection ground is the float/Decimal-mode argument.

conventions.topic: money - the minor-unit ratio is configuration
conventions.rule: 'The ratio is a one-way door... It is therefore a named configuration value, `CURRENCY_MINOR_UNIT_RATIO`, validated at boot and logged once. `100` never appears as a literal on the money path - not in a conversion, not in a test fixture, not in a seed script. Being a variable does not make it changeable; it is a named value so that it is visible and checkable.'
conventions.cite: PRD E8 S7.2; FR-ADR-036; Bible S-PAY-01
conventions.note: Boot validation is asserted: 'with CURRENCY_MINOR_UNIT_RATIO unset, 0, or non-integer the process exits non-zero before binding a port, stderr names the variable, and a connection to /health/live is refused'. FOR THE SCHEMA: the value 100 must not appear in a column name, a COMMENT ON, a CHECK expression, a generated column, or a seed insert. Bible S-PAY-01 greps for it: "rg -n '[*/]\s*100\b|\b100\s*[*/]' ... returns 0 hits".

conventions.rule: 'No per-row currency column. One currency exists, and a constant repeated on every row invites a mixed-currency sum nobody validates. A second currency would be a schema change, and it should be one.'
conventions.note: CURRENCY_CODE=INR is configuration, surfaced in API responses (`currency_code`), never a column.

conventions.rule: 'SUM() over a `bigint` column returns `numeric` in PostgreSQL, which arrives in Python as `Decimal` and mixes badly with `int` - cast back to `BigInteger` in the query.'
conventions.cite: PRD E8 S7.2; FR-ADR-043 Consequences; GOTCHAS.md 'Database & Postgres'; PRD E7 P-RPT-01 load-bearing point 2
conventions.note: Not a schema rule but it constrains every revenue query written against these columns. COALESCE(SUM(...), 0) is also load-bearing: 'SUM() over an empty set returns NULL, not zero.'

conventions.rule: 'No foreign key uses `ON DELETE CASCADE` on any path that can reach a booking. The default for every relationship is `ON DELETE RESTRICT`. A cascade is a delete that happens without anyone writing the word delete.' `ON DELETE SET NULL` on booking.user_id is named and rejected: it breaks SRC-001 §7.6 and FR-ADR-014 requires that foreign key non-null.
conventions.cite: FR-ADR-012; PRD E8 P-XCT-04 preconditions; PRD E5 (E5_account.md:885)
conventions.note: PRD E8 P-XCT-04 exception 4: 'An entity the booking references has been removed | cannot occur - ON DELETE RESTRICT prevents it, and the attempted delete fails.'

conventions.rule: 'Two admins editing the same row: optimistic concurrency with a `version` integer. The client sends the version it read; a mismatch returns 409 with "this was changed by someone else".' 'The `version` column adds one integer to four tables and one comparison to each admin update.'
conventions.note: The COUNT is stated ('four tables') but I did not find the four NAMED in one place. From E6 the versioned entities are movie, showtime, seat_category and screen (E6 governance row 27 says 'a seat has no `version` - EP-ADM-20 accepts none', which excludes `seat` and confirms the set is closed). The merge owner should confirm the four against the E6 cluster's output rather than take my inference. `seat` explicitly has NO version column.

conventions.rule: 'Alembic. A separate step. Never on boot, never automatically. There is no code path in the API or the worker that can apply a migration. Not at import, not in a lifespan hook, not in the entrypoint's default path, and not behind a `RUN_MIGRATIONS` flag - a flag would be set to true once, during an incident, and never set back.' 'The entrypoint takes a command argument. There are four: `api`, `worker`, `migrate` and `seed`.' The reason is a fact, not a preference: 'Alembic does not take an advisory lock. This is widely believed and it is not true, so two tasks booting together race on `alembic upgrade head`.'
conventions.cite: SRC-002 §7.8; PRD E8 S7.11; PRD E8 P-XCT-19; FR-ADR-062; GOTCHAS.md 'Alembic does NOT take an advisory lock'; Bible S-XCT-33
conventions.note: Machine-checkable in Bible S-XCT-33: "rg -in 'alembic' backend/app returns 0 hits"; a fifth entrypoint command exits non-zero naming the four; 'starting the image with api against a database one revision behind starts the process, returns 200 from /health/live and /health/ready, and returns 500 INTERNAL_ERROR at the first request touching a new column rather than failing at boot'.

conventions.topic: migrations - how the schema is applied
conventions.rule: Deploy order is one-directional: '1 snapshot (manual, persists beyond the 7-day automated window) / 2 migrate (one-off task, same image, command overridden) / 3 verify (the task exited 0) / 4 deploy (update the service to the new image).' Every migration must be backwards-compatible with the code currently running, because the old code runs against the new schema for that window. 'No down-migrations are written or run. Alembic's `downgrade` stub stays a stub that raises... A bad migration is corrected by a new forward migration.' 'Compose does not run migrations - no `depends_on` chain applies them and no service runs them on start, because automating it locally would remove the habit the deployed process depends on.'
conventions.cite: PRD E8 S7.11; PRD E8 P-XCT-19; PRD E8 P-XCT-20; Bible S-XCT-33
conventions.note: Three DDL-shaping consequences, all machine-asserted by Bible S-XCT-33: (1) 'every revision file's downgrade body is a single raise NotImplementedError, asserted by a test parsing each file under backend/migrations/versions with ast and finding the downgrade function's body is exactly one Raise node'; (2) "rg -n 'drop_column|drop_table|alter_column' backend/migrations/versions returns 0 hits" - forward-only, additive-only; (3) 'every revision file matching rg -l \'audit_log|booking_seat\' also matches rg -l \'# LOCK:\'' - a migration touching either of the two unbounded-growth tables carries a `# LOCK:` comment naming what it locks and for roughly how long. Also: 'The constraint is created before any seat row can exist' - Bible S-XCT-04 requires the booking_seat unique constraint to be created in the SAME single Phase 2 migration file that creates the table, 'so no earlier revision can have written a seat row without the constraint in place', and "rg -in 'drop_constraint|DROP CONSTRAINT' backend/migrations returns 0 hits".

conventions.rule: 'Email is the identity. Unique, case-insensitively. Stored as entered, compared and constrained on its lowercased form via a unique index on `lower(email)`. Storing a lowercased copy in a second column would be two fields to keep in step.'
conventions.note: NOT citext. The chosen mechanism is a functional unique index. Bible S-XCT-12 asserts it directly: 'a unique index exists on lower(email), asserted by SELECT indexdef FROM pg_indexes WHERE tablename = 'users' returning one CREATE UNIQUE INDEX containing lower(email), and the email is stored as entered, asserted by registering Nikhil@Example.invalid and reading the column back unchanged'. Note the table name in that SQL is `users` (plural), matching the brief's fixed list. The brief's type vocabulary offers `citext` - no document selects it, and FR-ADR-050 selects the alternative explicitly.

conventions.rule: 'The hyphens and the prefix are presentation. Storage is the eight characters, uppercase.' Alphabet is 30 characters: 23456789ABCDEFGHJKMNPQRSTVWXYZ. Presentation form is FR-XXXX-XXXX. 'The column carries a unique constraint. On a collision the insert fails and generation retries, bounded at five attempts.'
conventions.cite: FR-ADR-015; PRD E3 EP-PAY-01 201 body; Bible S-TKT-05
conventions.note: The COLUMN NAME is `reference`, not `reference_code` - Bible S-TKT-05 runs 'SELECT count(*) FROM booking WHERE reference=:r'. RESERVED (OPEN-REFCHAR-01): do not add a CHECK constraint on the alphabet. The stored 8-character form is never what crosses the wire: 'It is re-formatted at serialisation from the 8 characters stored on the booking row'.

conventions.rule: 'seat_id is an integer foreign key and seat_label carries the human form such as F7; a query comparing seat_id to a label string raises invalid input syntax'. Layout uses explicit `grid_row` and `grid_col` on the seat row, kept separate from `row_label` and `seat_number` on purpose. 'Aisles, gaps and non-seat space are represented by the absence of a seat at a coordinate, not by a placeholder row.'
conventions.note: RESERVED (OPEN-SEATALPHA-01, OPEN-SEATLABEL-01): no normalisation and no alphabet ban on row_label. OPEN-SEATLABEL-01 stops being fixable once the first showtime exists, which is Phase 2 - the same phase this schema lands in.

conventions.rule: 'SELECT count(*) FROM pg_indexes WHERE indexdef LIKE '%request_id%' AND indexdef LIKE 'CREATE UNIQUE INDEX%' returns 0 and rg -nP 'JOIN[^;]*request_id' backend/app returns 0 hits.'
conventions.note: A NEGATIVE index requirement and easy to violate by habit. request_id is a correlation string for log search, not a join key. It appears on audit_log and on outbox_message payloads; neither may carry a unique index on it. The request id format is asserted as ^[0-9a-f]{8}$ and 'an inbound X-Request-Id is never trusted'.

conventions.rule: 'No card data anywhere - not a column, not a log, not a fixture (SRC-003 OPEN-PAY-01).' 'No request schema in this epic accepts `status`, `cancelled_at`, `refund_amount_paise` or any similarly named field.' Bible S-PAY-10: 'no fee, tax or discount figure exists in any table'.
conventions.cite: SRC-003 OPEN-PAY-01; PRD E3 P-PAY-12; PRD E6 P-ADM-19; Bible S-PAY-10
conventions.note: Also forbidden by name in the audit payload: 'password_hash and everything derived from it never appear in `before` or `after`', and 'No poster bytes - before and after carry the S3 object key, not the image.'

conventions.rule: GOTCHAS.md names three places local Postgres and RDS differ: 'superuser, forced SSL, and the allowed extension list.' Only the first is specified anywhere.
conventions.cite: GOTCHAS.md 'Local Postgres gives you superuser; RDS never does'; PRD E8 S7.11 exception 4
conventions.note: No document names a single PostgreSQL extension, and no document specifies sslmode on DATABASE_URL. Two of the three named RDS divergences are therefore unaddressed by the schema. See gaps.

rounding_rule.rule:
seat_price_paise = (base_price_paise * (10000 + uplift_basis_points) + 5000) // 10000

`base_price_paise` is `showtime.base_price_paise`, set by the admin per showtime. `uplift_basis_points` is `seat_category.uplift_basis_points`, one basis point being 0.01%, applied **uniformly across every hall and every show** (`SRC-003 OPEN-PRICE-01`). `10000` is the basis-point denominator and `5000` is half of it; adding half the denominator before an integer floor division is integer half-up. Both are named constants. Standard is not a special case in code - it is a row whose uplift is `0`, and the same expression runs for it.

[P-PAY-04] `booking_total_paise` is the arithmetic sum of the already-rounded per-seat prices from `P-PAY-03`. **The total is never itself rounded, and the rounding rule is never applied to it.** It is stored on the booking row as `total_paise` (`FR-ADR-039`).

[E8 S7.2] **The invariant a reviewer checks is this:** rounding is applied per seat, the booking total is the sum of already-rounded per-seat prices, and **the total is never rounded**. If the per-seat prices shown on the seat map do not sum exactly to the total shown beside them, a second implementation exists somewhere.
rounding_rule.worked_example:
Showtime: `DEMO MOVIE 03`, Screen 4, `2026-08-21T19:30:00+05:30`.
`showtime.base_price_paise = 27500` (Rs 275.00).
Category uplifts, `ASSUMED` names (`SRC-003 OPEN-SEAT-01`): Standard `0`, Premium `1250` (12.5%), Recliner `3333` (33.33%).

Selection: **five seats - `F7`, `F8`, `F9` Premium and `J3`, `J4` Recliner.**

Premium, each of `F7`, `F8`, `F9`:

    (27500 * (10000 + 1250) + 5000) // 10000
    = (27500 * 11250 + 5000) // 10000
    = (309375000 + 5000) // 10000
    = 309380000 // 10000
    = 30938                                        ->  Rs 309.38

The exact value is `27500 * 1.1250 = 30937.5` - an exact half. Half-up takes it to `30938`. Half-even would give `30938` here too because `30938` is the even neighbour; case 3 below is where the two rules visibly disagree.

Recliner, each of `J3`, `J4`:

    (27500 * (10000 + 3333) + 5000) // 10000
    = (27500 * 13333 + 5000) // 10000
    = (366657500 + 5000) // 10000
    = 366662500 // 10000
    = 36666                                        ->  Rs 366.66

The exact value is `27500 * 1.3333 = 36665.75`. Half-up takes it to `36666`. Floor would give `36665`.

Standard, for completeness - no rounding occurs:

    (27500 * (10000 + 0) + 5000) // 10000 = 275005000 // 10000 = 27500   ->  Rs 275.00

[P-PAY-04] **The rule - round per seat, then sum:**

    Premium   30938 * 3 = 92814
    Recliner  36666 * 2 = 73332
    total               = 166146 paise            ->  Rs 1,661.46

**The wrong way - carry the exact values and round the total once:**

    Premium   30937.5 * 3 = 92812.5
    Recliner  36665.75 * 2 = 73331.5
    sum                    = 166144.0
    half-up                = 166144 paise         ->  Rs 1,661.44

**The difference is 2 paise.** `166146 - 166144 = 2`.

**Half-up against half-even, the case where they visibly disagree** (`FR-ADR-038`): a base of `25000` with a Recliner uplift of `3333` gives an exact `33332.5`. Half-up gives `33333`; half-even gives `33332`, because `33332` is the even neighbour. This project uses half-up, because it is what a person doing the arithmetic by hand produces, and the operator is also the client.
rounding_rule.cite: PRD E3 P-PAY-03 and P-PAY-04 (docs/03 PRD/sections/E3_checkout_payment.md:225-370); FR-ADR-038; PRD E8 S7.2; ADR ledger LED-038

retention.policy: Nothing is ever deleted. No pruning job, no retention window, no destructive cascade. 'Entities that stop being current are withdrawn, not removed.' The client's ruling was 'for now forever we'll change that later if i ask.' Storage grows without bound against a 20 GB free-tier RDS volume; that belongs in the runbook 'with a figure to watch, not as an alarm nobody configured.'
retention.cite: SRC-003 OPEN-OPS-02; FR-ADR-012; PRD E8 P-XCT-11; PRD S2 §scope-guard table ('prune old idempotency records | nothing is ever deleted (FR-ADR-012)')

retention.policy: Never expired and never deleted. 'A key that expires is a key whose retry after the window creates a second booking.' A reused key is refused permanently with 422 IDEMPOTENCY_KEY_REUSED - 'a permanent refusal, because the record is never deleted.' A record does roll back with its transaction when the confirm fails, which is not a deletion but a never-committed row.
retention.cite: PRD E8 P-XCT-22 preconditions table ('Expire idempotency records | nothing - the record is never expired'); PRD E3 P-PAY-09 (E3_checkout_payment.md:730); PRD E3 EP-PAY-01 idempotency block ('The record is never expired and never deleted.')

retention.policy: Rows are never deleted, including poison ones: 'A message arrives whose `topic` is neither `receipt.send` nor `password_reset.send` | logged at ERROR with the topic and request_id, not deleted; redelivery carries it to the dead letter queue.' A stuck `pending` row is relayed, not swept: 'the worker's existing receive loop checks for pending rows older than a short threshold before each poll. Work on a loop that already exists, not a timer.'
retention.cite: FR-ADR-031; PRD E8 P-XCT-22 preconditions table; PRD E4 P-TKT-11 exception 7

retention.policy: Append-only and grows forever. 'The audit table only ever grows. That is correct - an audit log that prunes is not an audit log - and it is the largest table this system will have.' Enforced at the grant level, not by convention. A migration touching it carries a `# LOCK:` comment.
retention.cite: FR-ADR-012 Consequences; FR-ADR-019; PRD E8 S7.3; Bible S-XCT-07; Bible S-XCT-33

retention.policy: No document states that a reset token row is ever deleted, so FR-ADR-012's blanket rule applies and rows accumulate. Expiry is a COMPARISON, not a deletion: 'expires_at = created_at + PASSWORD_RESET_TTL_SECONDS, compared against the injected clock'. A spent token is marked (`used_at`), not removed. A failed send clears the claim in place: UPDATE password_reset_token SET email_claimed_at = NULL WHERE id = :id AND email_sent_at IS NULL.
retention.cite: FR-ADR-012; PRD E5 P-ACC-07 (E5_account.md:744); PRD E4 (E4_receipt_entry.md:1304); GOTCHAS.md 'Three columns on password_reset_token'

retention.policy: THE ONLY ROWS THE NO-DELETE RULE DOES NOT REACH. 'Rows that carry no history are current state and may be removed: a manager-to-screen assignment (FR-ADR-011), an expired Redis lock, a cache entry. The rule is about the record of what happened, not about every row in the database.' A seat may also be deleted pre-showtime only (audit action `seat.deleted`, P-ADM-13). PRD E8 P-XCT-11 scopes the claim: 'The product is not delete-free in general - the two deletions that do exist are unreachable from a booking by their own preconditions.'
retention.cite: FR-ADR-012 'Where this rule does not reach'; PRD E8 P-XCT-04 preconditions; PRD E6 P-ADM-19 action table (seat.deleted, manager.screen_unassigned); PRD E6 EP-ADM-21

retention.policy: Holds live only in Redis and expire by the key's own TTL. 'A seat becomes available because its key is gone. No sweeper, no reconciler.' There is no PostgreSQL table a hold check could fall back to - Bible S-PAY-08 asserts the absence.
retention.cite: PRD E8 P-XCT-22 preconditions table; FR-ADR-025; Bible S-PAY-08; brief's reserved list (OPEN-HOLDRECOVER-01)

gaps.what: THE RESTRICTED DATABASE ROLE HAS NO NAME. Every document that requires it describes it by role rather than by identifier: 'the application database role', 'the application role', 'a restricted application role without superuser', 'the compose stack creates an application role without superuser'. The two machine-checkable assertions both dodge the name by using `current_user` (Bible S-XCT-07: 'grantee = current_user'; Bible S-XCT-33: 'rolname = current_user'), which passes whatever the role is called.
gaps.why_it_matters: The schema package has to emit a `CREATE ROLE <name>` and `GRANT ... TO <name>`, and the compose stack has to put that name into DATABASE_URL. Picking a name is a judgement call and reversible, but picking it SILENTLY means six other artefacts (docker-compose.yml, the migration, the SSM parameter for the deployed DATABASE_URL, the Zone C RDS specification in docs/30 Deployment/, the seed script, the runbook) each pick their own and only agree by luck. This is the item the brief called the most valuable, and the honest answer is that the documents require the role and never name it.
gaps.where_you_looked: GOTCHAS.md (whole file); SRC-001, SRC-002, SRC-003, OPEN_QUESTIONS (grep for restricted/GRANT/REVOKE/superuser/CREATE ROLE returned ZERO hits in docs/00 SourceOfTruth/); all 73 FR-ADR files; all 12 PRD section files; FrontRow_Bible.csv (all 200 criteria). No document in the repository contains a single SQL GRANT, REVOKE or CREATE ROLE statement.

gaps.what: WHETHER THE MIGRATION RUNS AS THE SAME ROLE AS THE APPLICATION - and if it does, whether that role can satisfy the audit_log grant assertion at all. E8 S7.11 and P-XCT-19 say the migrate task 'reads DATABASE_URL the same way' as the service, which reads as one role. But Bible S-XCT-07 asserts that 'SELECT privilege_type FROM information_schema.table_privileges WHERE table_name = 'audit_log' AND grantee = current_user' returns EXACTLY the two rows INSERT and SELECT. In PostgreSQL a table's owner is granted all privileges on it implicitly, and those self-grants ARE rows in information_schema.table_privileges - so a single role that migrates (and therefore owns audit_log) and then connects as the application would return seven rows, not two, and the acceptance criterion fails against a correct-looking implementation.
gaps.why_it_matters: There are exactly two ways out and no document picks one: (a) two roles - a migration/owner role and a restricted application role, with the migration running GRANT INSERT, SELECT ON audit_log TO <app> and nothing else; or (b) one role that owns the table and REVOKEs UPDATE, DELETE, TRUNCATE from itself in the migration. Both work; they produce different docker-compose files, different DATABASE_URLs, different SSM parameters and a different Zone C RDS specification for the client. Choosing wrong is discovered when S-XCT-07 goes red in Phase 2, or - worse - when someone 'fixes' the criterion instead of the schema. (The PostgreSQL owner-privilege behaviour above is REASONED from the documented semantics, not observed on this project; no code and no database exist yet.)
gaps.where_you_looked: PRD E8 S7.11, S7.3, P-XCT-19, P-XCT-20, P-XCT-03; FR-ADR-019, FR-ADR-062, FR-ADR-012, FR-ADR-017; Bible S-XCT-07, S-XCT-33, S-ADM-02; SRC-002 §7.8; GOTCHAS.md

gaps.what: THE GRANTS FOR EVERY TABLE EXCEPT audit_log ARE UNSPECIFIED. audit_log is the only table any document constrains at the grant level. Nothing says whether the application role gets DELETE on the tables where a delete IS permitted (manager_screen_assignment, seat pre-showtime), whether it gets TRUNCATE anywhere (it should not), whether it gets USAGE on the identity sequences, or what the default privileges are for tables a later migration creates.
gaps.why_it_matters: FR-ADR-012 makes 'nothing is ever deleted' a design rule enforced only by the absence of DELETE statements in application code - which is convention, exactly the thing E8 S7.3 refuses to accept for audit_log ('append-only, enforced and not merely intended'). The stricter and cheaper option is to withhold DELETE from the application role on every table except the two where deletion is ruled legal, which would make FR-ADR-012 enforced the same way FR-ADR-019 is. Adopting a stricter option needs no signature (Art III.10) - but it is a decision, it belongs in the data model package, and no document has made it.
gaps.where_you_looked: All ADRs, all PRD sections, the Bible, GOTCHAS.md, the source-of-truth documents

gaps.what: WHICH TABLES CARRY updated_at. The rule is 'tables that mutate carry updated_at' and the Bible explicitly hands the list to this goal: 'which tables those are is a judgement that follows from the data model and is checked there rather than here' (S-XCT-06).
gaps.why_it_matters: It is deliberately delegated rather than missing, so it is the merge owner's call rather than an Article X row - but it must be DERIVED from the five clusters' mutation paths (does any endpoint UPDATE this table?) rather than applied uniformly. Putting updated_at on booking, booking_seat, payment or audit_log would be wrong twice over: those rows are never updated after their transaction, and on audit_log the application role has no UPDATE privilege at all.
gaps.where_you_looked: FR-ADR-012 Consequences; PRD E8 P-XCT-04; Bible S-XCT-06 (line 171); grep for updated_at across PRD, ADRs and the Bible returned exactly one substantive hit

gaps.what: WHETHER updated_at IS MAINTAINED BY A DATABASE TRIGGER OR BY THE APPLICATION. No document says. The only trigger discussion in the product is E8 S7.3's refusal of one for audit_log, on grounds specific to audit_log ('a trigger cannot know the acting user or the request id').
gaps.why_it_matters: It bears directly on the injected-clock rule. An application-maintained updated_at would naturally be written from the injected clock, making it controllable in tests; a `BEFORE UPDATE` trigger calling now() is not injectable at all. FR-ADR-018 already permits `DEFAULT now()` for created_at/updated_at as ROW METADATA specifically because nothing asserts against it - which is an argument that the trigger route is acceptable here and only here. But that is an inference from a sentence about defaults, not a ruling about triggers, and it should be decided in the data model rather than left to whoever writes the first mutating table.
gaps.where_you_looked: FR-ADR-018; PRD E8 S7.3, S7.19; grep for 'trigger' across all PRD sections (every other hit is an exception-table column header meaning 'what causes this')

gaps.what: THE FORM OF EVERY STATUS/ROLE VOCABULARY - PostgreSQL enum type, text + CHECK, or lookup table - IS UNSPECIFIED for users.role, booking.status, payment.state, outbox_message.status, outbox_message.topic and receipt_dispatch.status. The documents are precise about the VALUES and silent about the MECHANISM. Only three vocabularies have their form ruled, and all three are ruled as lookup tables and against enums: seat_category (FR-ADR-016), language and certification (FR-ADR-021).
gaps.why_it_matters: The reasoning that rejected a PostgreSQL enum for seat categories transfers only partly. FR-ADR-016 gives three grounds: 'Adding a value to a PostgreSQL enum is a migration, the values cannot carry the price uplift, and OPEN-SEAT-01 was answered "you pick" - which is exactly the kind of answer that gets revised.' The second ground (carrying data) does not apply to a status; the first and third do apply to users.role, which is PROVISIONAL under SRC-003 C-1 and whose reversal to three roles is described in five separate places as removing 'the manager role value'. Removing a value from a PostgreSQL enum is not a migration you can write forward-only, and this project writes no down-migrations and forbids alter_column. That argues for text + CHECK over a native enum for role at least - but it is a decision, not something the documents made.

If it is unconstrained text, the column is a free-text status column - the thing FR-ADR-019 refuses for audit actions. gaps.what: FORCED SSL AND THE ALLOWED EXTENSION LIST - two of the three RDS/local divergences GOTCHAS.md names - are unaddressed. No document specifies sslmode on DATABASE_URL, and no document names a single PostgreSQL extension.
gaps.why_it_matters: GOTCHAS.md's whole point is that these are the three places a migration that works locally fails on RDS, and the mitigation ('build against the restricted role from day one') only covers the first. A migration that does `CREATE EXTENSION citext` or `pg_trgm` would pass locally and fail on RDS at exactly the moment the client runs the one-off migrate task - the failure the local restricted role was supposed to make impossible. The schema should either use no extension at all (achievable: FR-ADR-050 already chose `lower(email)` over citext, and nothing else in the product needs one) and say so, or name the ones it needs and put them on the AWS prep queue.

notes: *** `stress_operator` IS NOT A DATABASE ROLE. *** The brief asked what it is and what it may do. It is `STRESS_OPERATOR`, an ENVIRONMENT VARIABLE read by scripts/stress_seats.py, and it names the HUMAN who ran the concurrency proof. Bible S-XCT-01: 'the script prints its outcome as one JSON object on stdout carrying operator, run_at as an ISO-8601 UTC instant, base_url, winners, losers, spread_ms, distinct_users and unique_constraint_violations, reads operator from STRESS_OPERATOR which has no default, and exits non-zero naming STRESS_OPERATOR when it is unset, because an unattributed undated claim that it was run is not evidence.' It appears in exactly three Bible criteria (S-XCT-01, S-XCT-02, S-XCT-18) and nowhere else in the repository. It grants nothing, owns nothing, and must NOT appear in the schema. Anyone who models it as a database role has created a role the product does not have and missed that the real one is unnamed.

THE SINGLE HIGHEST-VALUE ITEM FOR THE MERGE: primary keys are `bigint GENERATED ALWAYS AS IDENTITY`, database-generated, per FR-ADR-017 - and the brief told all six clusters to default to application-generated `uuid`. If five clusters returned uuid columns, the merged schema is wrong on every table and wrong specifically on the oversell guard, which FR-ADR-017 names as the reason for the decision. Check every cluster's `id` and every `*_id` foreign key before assembling datamodel.json.

The four money columns Bible S-PAY-10 calls 'the complete set' are complete only for the three tables its SQL scans (booking, booking_seat, payment). `showtime.base_price_paise` is a fifth money column and is required to be `bigint NOT NULL with no default` by P-PAY-03 exception 1 and FR-ADR-037. Do not read S-PAY-10's 'complete set' as the product-wide inventory; read it as what it says - no fee, tax or discount figure exists in any table.

`booking_seat.uplift_basis_points_applied` and `seat_category.uplift_basis_points` are integers in basis points, NOT money, and their names deliberately do not end `_paise`. 'Basis points and not a decimal percentage, because a decimal reintroduces a non-integer type into the one calculation this project cares most about getting exactly right' (P-ADM-11). Server-side validation: both `>= 0`, integer; 'The function accepts nothing else; a float argument is a type error, not a rounded result.'

The payment status column is named `state`, not `status` - Bible S-RPT-16 requires an index on `payment(state)` and S-PAY-05 runs `SELECT state, amount_paise, idempotency_key FROM payment`. Every other status-like column in the product is `status`. The inconsistency is in the documents, not in my reading, and 200 criteria will run against it. Do not normalise it.

The foreign key direction between booking and payment is `booking.payment_id -> payment.id` and NOT the reverse, 'because the payment row exists before the booking row does'. Bible S-RPT-16 asserts the absence of the wrong column: 'SELECT count(*) FROM information_schema.columns WHERE table_schema = 'public' AND table_name='payment' AND column_name='booking_id' returning 0, the column not existing', plus "rg -n 'payment\.booking_id' backend/app backend/migrations returning 0 hits".

TWO unique constraints on `(showtime_id, seat_id)` exist, on TWO different tables, and they are not interchangeable. `booking_seat (showtime_id, seat_id)` is the oversell guard - total, never partial, no WHERE clause, and it is what the red-proof drill drops and restores. `showtime_seat (showtime_id, seat_id)` 'only prevents one seat being listed twice on one showtime'. P-ADM-14 says it in terms: 'That unique index is not the oversell guard, and nothing may treat it as one... Two tables, two constraints, two different jobs; neither substitutes for the other, and a reader who conflates them will believe the oversell guard has been moved.'

The oversell constraint is TOTAL, not partial. FR-ADR-024: 'No `WHERE status <> 'cancelled'` clause. FR-ADR-013 rules out cancellation in v1, so a partial index would exclude a state that cannot occur while making the guard conditional. If cancellation is ever added, this constraint must be revisited before it.' Bible S-PAY-09 asserts 'SELECT indexdef FROM pg_indexes WHERE tablename='booking_seat' returns exactly ONE UNIQUE index, its definition contains (showtime_id, seat_id) and contains no WHERE clause' - so booking_seat may carry no second unique index of any kind.

The audit action vocabulary is closed and is enforced in APPLICATION code, not in the database: 'the closed vocabulary is the module-level tuple AUDIT_ACTIONS in backend/app/domain/audit.py, and a value outside it is refused with 500 INTERNAL_ERROR at a boundary check that runs BEFORE the transaction opens' (Bible S-XCT-07). E8 P-XCT-03 exception 4 confirms the check precedes BEGIN and E6 records that E8's placement was adopted as the stricter of two published readings. I recorded form='check' for it because the vocabulary is genuinely closed and machine-enforced; if the data model also adds a database CHECK it must be kept in step with that tuple, which is a second place the list lives. Note that the boundary check is asserted by 'a connection-level statement listener that records ZERO statements for that request' - a database CHECK would produce a statement and could fail that assertion. Prefer no database CHECK on audit_log.action.

The outbox payload guard is the ONE place the Bible explicitly hands GOAL_08 a free choice of mechanism: 'this criterion asserts the observable outcome and names no mechanism, so GOAL_08 may implement the guard as a CHECK constraint, a trigger or application validation' (S-TKT-05). The observable outcome is that an outbox_message with topic='receipt.render', or a receipt.send payload with a fifth key, or one missing message_version, DOES NOT COMMIT. Required payload key sets, sorted: receipt.send = {booking_id, dispatch_seq, message_version, request_id}; password_reset.send = {message_version, request_id, reset_token_id, user_id}. 'the payload text contains no @ character, no seat label and no amount.'

Seat `state` (available|held|sold) is a COMPUTED API-RESPONSE FIELD, not a column - it is derived per request from booking_seat rows and Redis lock keys. `seat.is_active` IS a column and is deliberately NOT a fourth state value: 'a fifth enum value would make "retired" and "sold" mutually exclusive', 'a seat can be both retired and sold without either fact being lost'. Do not create a seat.state column.

No latency budget exists anywhere in the product and none may be invented. P-BRW-14: 'No frozen source states a latency budget of any kind - no p50, no p95, no time-to-first-byte, no render budget, no frames-per-second target for the seat map, and no throughput figure. None is written in this document. A number invented here would be indistinguishable from a ruled one three documents later, which is exactly the failure this project already produced once with the seven-minute hold.' Consequently the index list above is derived ONLY from queries the documents actually state - six from the dashboard query in Bible S-RPT-16, the two oversell/roster uniques, the two identity lookups (lower(email), booking.reference), one per-booking dispatch unique, and one idempotency-key unique. I listed no speculative index. In particular I did NOT add an index for movie browse/filter/sort (published_at, display_from, display_until, language_id, genre) despite FR-ADR-021 describing that predicate, because no document states the query's performance requirement and FR-ADR-030 answers browse latency with a 60-second cache instead - the merge owner should decide that deliberately rather than inherit my omission as a ruling.
One NEGATIVE index requirement, easy to violate: request_id must carry NO unique index and no index whose definition mentions it (Bible S-XCT-24). It is a log-correlation string, not a join key.

I found NO contradiction with the no-scheduler rule anywhere in the retention material - and I looked for one specifically, because the brief expected one. The documents anticipated it and closed every route in a single table (P-XCT-22 preconditions): holds expire by Redis TTL; idempotency records are never expired; nothing is pruned; stuck outbox rows are relayed on the worker's EXISTING receive loop; the seat_locks_held counter is reconciled by a bounded SCAN on that same loop; cache entries expire by their own TTL. Every one of those replaces a timer with either an expiry the datastore performs itself or work folded into a process that already runs. Nothing in the retention set requires a periodic job.

docs/06 DataModel/ is empty and GOAL_08 is the first artefact to name a database role, choose an enum form, or emit a GRANT. Three of the gaps above (the role name, the migration-role question, the grants beyond audit_log) are decisions that will be made by whoever writes the first migration whether or not anyone notices. They are non-reserved technical questions and the build session may decide them - but each should be ONE `[JUDGMENT CALL]` line, not a silent choice inside a migration file, because the role name in particular has to match a Zone C specification the client will build RDS against and a docker-compose file the client will read.

Two independent readings in this report are REASONED, NOT OBSERVED, and are labelled where they appear: (a) that a PostgreSQL table owner's implicit privileges appear as rows in information_schema.table_privileges and would break Bible S-XCT-07's 'exactly two rows' assertion if the migration role and the application role are the same - this follows from documented PostgreSQL semantics, and no database exists on this project to check it against; (b) that FR-ADR-035's 'four tables' carrying a `version` column are movie, showtime, seat_category and screen - inferred from E6's endpoint set and from its explicit statement that `seat` has none. Neither has been verified against running code, because no application code exists.
